title: Polyatomic Ions
short: Groups such as NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ act as single ions; use parentheses when you need more than one.
trouble: Students drop the parentheses and write CaNO₃₂, or change a subscript inside the polyatomic ion to balance the charge.

blocks.html: Some ions are groups of atoms bonded together that carry one charge as a unit, like the nitrate ion, $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$. They behave like single ions in ionic compounds: the group stays whole, and you balance charges just as before.

A polyatomic ion keeps its own name and formula. To write a compound, balance the charges; if you need more than one of a polyatomic ion, put it in parentheses with the count outside: calcium nitrate is $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$. Never change the subscripts inside the ion.

blocks.cap: Common polyatomic ions. Pattern: an -ite ion has one oxygen fewer than the -ate ion with the same charge.

blocks.html: Inside a polyatomic ion the atoms are held by covalent bonds, and the whole group has a set number of electrons, so its charge is fixed. Changing $\mathrm{NO_3}$ to $\mathrm{NO_6}$ would describe a different (and impossible) particle. Parentheses tell the reader that the subscript outside multiplies the whole group: $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$ has 1 Ca, 2 N and 6 O.

blocks.title: Ammonium sulfate
blocks.q: Write the formula of ammonium sulfate.
steps: Two ammonium ions (+2) balance one sulfate (−2).

blocks.title: Counting atoms
blocks.q: How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of $\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}$?
steps: Each sulfate has 4 O, and the 3 outside multiplies the whole group.

steps: Three $\mathrm{OH^-}$ carry −3, so the iron ion is +3.

blocks.html: Dropping the parentheses and writing $\mathrm{CaNO_{32}}$, or changing a subscript inside the polyatomic ion to balance the charge ($\mathrm{CaNO_6}$). Keep each ion whole, decide how many you need, and only then add parentheses and a count.
